---
title: "Binary Search on Answer: Search a Monotone Predicate"
description: "A mathematical technique worth memorising for algorithm interviews."
---

## Recognition trigger

Minimum feasible capacity, speed, days or maximum achievable threshold.

## Problem to think through

**How can you search an unknown answer when no sorted array is provided?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
F(x)=0\ (x<x^\star),\qquad F(x)=1\ (x\ge x^\star)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** F(x) is a Boolean feasibility test, 0 means impossible, 1 possible, and x* is the smallest feasible threshold. x is the candidate answer.

**Substitute actual values:** Suppose a worker needs 17 hours of work spread across d days with max 5 hours/day. Feasibility is F(d)=[5d≥17]. F(3)=0 because 15<17; F(4)=1 because 20≥17. The smallest feasible day count is 4.

## Why the derivation is valid

If a plan is possible with capacity x, it remains possible with any larger capacity under the same constraints. That creates a false-to-true boundary, so testing a midpoint discards half the candidate range. Binary search needs O(log R) predicate calls for an integer range of size R.

## What could invalidate it?

You MUST prove monotonicity. Some problems are feasible only for isolated values; using binary search there silently skips answers. Guard against overflow in midpoint arithmetic in fixed-width languages.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Define F(x), prove its true/false boundary, find infeasible/feasible bounds, then halve the interval.**

Reconstruct the proof from the example rather than memorising the code.

**Interview problems:** Koko Eating Bananas; Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days.

**Research reference:** [Read the mathematical method](https://cp-algorithms.com/num_methods/binary_search.html). The worked numbers and explanation are independently written.
